title: Zechariah 1:1–6
context: The book opens with a date “in the eighth month, in the second year of Darius,” when the LORD’s word came to “the prophet Zechariah the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo” (1:1). This places him among the returned exiles, alongside Haggai (compare Haggai 1:1 and Ezra 5:1, where he is called “the son of Iddo”). The LORD speaks through the prophet, recalling his displeasure with their ancestors and calling: “Return to me… and I will return to you” (1:3). The former prophets had called the fathers to turn, but they did not listen; yet God’s words overtook them, and they confessed that the LORD had dealt with them as he purposed (1:4–6). The same call appears in Malachi 3:7, and James 4:8 voices a related invitation; on how grace and response relate in such invitations, see the James 4:8 box. Shared ground: both traditions read the opening as a sincere call to repentance, grounded in God’s faithfulness to his word.

verses.text: In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the LORD’s word came to the prophet Zechariah the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Zechariah in the second year of Darius. Arminian readers note that the date places the prophet among the returned exiles, called to encourage a discouraged community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precise dating as anchoring God’s word in history, alongside Haggai (compare Haggai 1:1). Shared ground: both traditions read the superscription as introducing a prophet sent to the rebuilding community after the exile.

verses.text: “The LORD was very displeased with your fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he was very displeased with their fathers. Arminian readers see the past recalled as a warning, showing where earlier generations went wrong.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s displeasure as just, a reminder of why the exile came. Both traditions read the verse as setting the stage for the call to return, grounding it in honest memory of the past.

verses.text: Therefore tell them, the LORD of Armies says: ‘Return to me,’ says the LORD of Armies, ‘and I will return to you,’ says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says, Return to me, and I will return to you. Arminian readers see a genuine invitation that calls for a real human response, met by God’s gracious return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call as the means through which God draws his people back to himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the promise as sincere, and they compare Malachi 3:7.

verses.text: Don’t you be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets proclaimed, saying: The LORD of Armies says, ‘Return now from your evil ways and from your evil doings;’ but they didn’t hear nor listen to me, says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The people are not to be like their fathers, who did not listen when the former prophets called them to turn. Arminian readers see the danger of repeating the refusal of earlier generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as summarizing the message of the earlier prophets and the hardness that met it. Both traditions read the warning as an appeal to learn from history and to respond where the fathers did not.

verses.text: Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks where the fathers are now, and whether the prophets live forever. Arminian readers see a reminder that human life is short, and the time to respond is limited.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast between mortal people and the abiding word set up for the next verse. Shared ground: both traditions read the questions as pointing to the passing of generations, while God’s word endures.

verses.text: But my words and my decrees, which I commanded my servants the prophets, didn’t they overtake your fathers? “Then they repented and said, ‘Just as the LORD of Armies determined to do to us, according to our ways and according to our practices, so he has dealt with us.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: God’s words overtook the fathers, and they repented, saying the LORD dealt with them as he purposed. Arminian readers see repentance coming after judgment, when the fathers finally acknowledged their ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s decrees accomplished just as he determined, compare Isaiah 55:11 by reference. Both traditions read the verse as testimony that God’s word proves true, and that honest confession follows its fulfillment.
